title: On Hope
author: Claire Stoneman
summary: Writing as a school leader in a challenging context, Stoneman opens with a personal reflection on hope, prompted by a sign in a neighbour's window and by memories of her late father. She then pivots to the professional question of what hope can and cannot do in a school. Her answer is that hope is a buffer on hard days but never a strategy: children do not get good outcomes, teaching, behaviour, curriculum or attendance because someone hopes for them. What produces sustained improvement is relentless, dogged graft over months and years, built on careful systems that are reviewed and sometimes thrown out. She argues that leaders must ignore noise and keep what happens in classrooms the main thing, even as the buffets of leadership make that hard. The piece closes on her resolve to lead with hope as a buffer and expectation as a whetstone.
points: Stoneman separates hope as emotional buffer from the plans, precision, systems and people that actually produce results in schools.
Sustainable improvement in challenging contexts takes years of insistent graft rather than short bursts of inspiration.
Systems deserve regular review, and those that do not work should be discarded rather than defended.
School leaders must deliberately ignore noise and keep classroom practice as the main thing, which is hardest when leadership is most demanding.
She names the toll of leading in challenging contexts, which has grown post-Covid, while insisting that difficulty is not an excuse.
quotes: On a professional level, hope is simply not enough. I can’t hope the children in my school into getting good outcomes. I can’t hope for effective teaching.
In schools, hope may be the buoy on hard days but, my goodness, plans, precision, systems and - most importantly, people - are the enablers.
It takes graft - and in schools in challenging contexts a relentless, dogged, insistent graft over weeks and months and years - to sustainably improve.
It takes systems, the careful application of systems, the review of systems, and the chucking out of systems that simply don’t work.
At the risk of sounding pithy, it means keeping the main thing - what’s happening in classrooms, in front of kids - the main thing.
Leadership of schools in challenging contexts is unbelievably, unremittingly hard, and with societal shifts and erosion post-Covid, it has become harder.
